meaningMnemonic: See the mouth and long, fang-like teeth of this alligator , which is facing to the right? You wouldn't want to get your hand stuck in there, that's for sure.
See how tall the stalks are with little bushy things at the top? It kind of looks like bamboo , if you use your imagination.

You'll have to complete the line on the right side in your mind, but see the rectangle bed and the pillows? This is totally a bed. That missing line is where you pulled back the covers when you got up this morning.
Doesn't this look like someone on their knees, holding their clasped hands out and begging for something (forgiveness, their life, a promotion, etc.)? That's why this radical is known as the beggar .
There's a cross branching off of this stool. Since it's branching out, we'll just call this the branch radical. I guess the tree this stool was made of is coming back to life in the form of a branch.
Doesn't this look like a top-down view of the frame of a car ? There are the axles at the top and bottom, and the body in the middle between them. That's why this is the car radical.

Remember the guy from the big radical? Here he's bending his arms at the elbow to fasten some kind of belt, right across the center of his body. It's one of those belts that just goes across your waist, which is actually perfect for such a big guy, since he really needs to secure his center (of gravity).

This radical looks like a person with a long dress running behind them. That's because they're all dressed up to go to a ceremony . You usually have to wear a long dress (or something formal) if you're going to a big ceremony, right? So when you see this radical, think of all the different ceremonies you might have to go to in your life and what you'll need to wear.
See the cliff ? It's facing to the left. What do you think this cliff is jutting out over? Maybe an ocean, or a valley? Cliffs love to jut out over things like that.

This is the ear radical, since it looks like an ear. As much as a radical can, anyway. Those two middle lines are the ridges that guide the sound into your ear, and the lines that stick out to the right are where the ear attaches to your head. If you think about it, ears are just eyes that see sound. Whoa, dude… That explains the eye ( 目 ) and ear ( 耳 ) radical resemblance. Just remember this one is "ear" because ears stick out, just like the lines sticking out of the side of this radical.

This is the radical for energy . If you imagine a train under this radical, then the lines would be steam bursting out of it, flowing back from the front of the train (on the left) as it goes chugging along. Steam was the best way to generate energy back in the day, you know? That's why this is the radical for energy.

See the little things sticking out of the ground? Those little things are pretty little flowers . You could also see this as a little flower crown, especially since this radical almost always appears at the top of a kanji.

This is the foot radical. See the person doing a flying dragon kick to the right? What do they hit the target with? Obviously their foot. Imagine that foot coming straight at your face. At that point, your only hope is that it's clean. Nobody wants a foot to the face, especially not a filthy foot.

Sure, this forehead is a bit square, but that's because it's the top part of the head ( 冂 ) radical. This is just the forehead part of that! You can even imagine this as the forehead of Frankenstein's monster, since his forehead was pretty square too. Also, don't confuse this for a roof. You know this is a forehead and not a roof because this doesn't have a cute little chimney sticking out of the top. Foreheads definitely don't have chimneys.

You have a roof on top of what looks like a volcano. What's the roof covering? It's definitely covering the hole at the top. I guess someone thought if they built a roof on the hole, none of the lava could come out. But isn't there a hole in the chimney? Guess their theory had some holes in it… Oh no, now lava is coming through the hole. RUN!!! RUN!!!!!!!!
Can you see the horns ? You could put these horns on anything. Donkeys, people, monkeys, and so on. That's exactly what we'll be doing when we learn kanji that have horns too.

This looks like the middle radical on top of a sideways leaf. What can you often find sitting on the middle of a leaf? An insect . Insects looove sitting right in the middle of leaves. That's why this is the insect radical.

This is the inside radical, since it looks like a person ( 人 ) inside a… head ( 冂 )? I guess if you think about it, every person is sort of trapped inside their own head. Imagine a second, tinier version of you sitting up inside that head of yours, like a mecha pilot. Yep, that's real you. The you inside .

This radical technically means person (like 人 ), but we're going to shift the meaning a little bit. It's kind of like the person radical, but it's taller and skinnier, standing above the others and raising its fist to lead them. That's why this is a leader , not a regular person.

The leader ( ｲ ) radical has a little something extra on top of him — he's got a casual cap on because it's his day off. And what does he like to do on his day off? He likes to loiter . Look at him just loitering around. What a loiterer.

A rice paddy needs power, and that power comes from a man . Picture a rice paddy full of thick, wet mud. It's no easy field to work in, but this powerful man will bend over to rake and hoe tirelessly to make sure it thrives. What a man!

The king is hovering a drop of water over his head. He's acquired the ability to manipulate water at will, making him the master of all water! If you think about how all life depends on water, that really makes him the master of everything…
Have you ever used one of those triangular rulers? This looks just like one of those, because this is the measurement radical. Just think of all the angles you could measure with this thing!

This looks like a regular arrow, but it's not . Let's call it the "not arrow." It can not move forward, because it's been stopped by some kind of line above it. Every arrow wants to fly, but this one is not going anywhere. Look at it, being all negated like that. Well, that's just what this radical does. It nots things.

You have two lines with legs below them. And what is that bit above the legs? Well, it's where you came from — your origin . Yep, between two legs is where you originated, no matter how you look at it.
Obviously, this looks just like the good ol' 3.14 something-something all people are supposed to learn about. It's the math symbol that has to do with circles... pi !

This is a few plates drying on a rack. They're stacked together in a line. Imagine reaching out and grabbing one of those plates for yourself. And you only need one, so let's call this radical plate .

A pile of dirt fell on you and now your legs and (scuba) fins are sticking out from under it, turning red . You know, because you've been stuck in the sun so long. Everything's all sunburned and red. Can scuba fins get a sunburn? Yeah, when it's red hot outside. That's why this means "red."

This is the radical for rice . Specifically raw rice, like the grain that grows out of the ground when rice is raw and fresh. When rice is particularly ripe, it'll kind of look like this at the top of the stalks. See the long leaves and the little rice tufts at the top? That's why this radical is "rice."

The samurai radical looks a lot like the dirt radical. The difference is this one has a longer top horizontal line, which is for those broad warrior shoulders. The bottom line is also shorter, since it's the little cushion the samurai is sitting on. Samurai didn't just fight, you know. They sat on cushions and wrote poems and stuff too. This is a very sensitive samurai.
This eye has legs, since you have to let your eyes run over something in order to see it. That's why those eyes need legs — to see. They're wandering eyes, they want to see the world!!
This radical looks like a shellfish . What looks like the eye radical is its long spiral shell. The bottom part that looks like fins is its little legs poking out, helping the shellfish move around.
On the ground there are a bunch of spikes coming out. You wouldn't want to step on those, now would you?

This radical looks like some sort of spirit . It faces to the left with a big hood over its head, and creepy arms slanting downward at the sides. Can you picture it? If not, just think of this as the katakana character for "ne." Ne for necromancer, bringing back spirits from the grave! OooooOOoooOoo!

In some poop you find something small. You lean in, carefully pull it out, and realize it's a thread . What's that doing there? Well, it came from a cat, and cats love to eat thread when you aren't looking. And floss and hoodie strings and mouse tails… But this time, just thread.
This radical looks like an umbrella , specifically just the handle part. A good old curvy umbrella handle, so you can hang that umbrella on your arm when it stops raining.
Use your imagination to draw a circle outside this shape. The grids from the radical start to look like longitude and latitude lines on a globe, don't they? That's why this is the world .
The bamboo radical and the bamboo kanji are exactly the same! Hints Just make sure you know your radicals!
readingMnemonic: Today is free bamboo day, so just take ( たけ ) all the bamboo you want. Hints Really take as much bamboo as you could possibly hold. Take some bamboo, then take some more, and take more… It’s free after all.

meaningMnemonic: The radical car and the kanji car are exactly the same. Hints Make sure you study your radicals... though don't do it while driving.
readingMnemonic: When we need to remember the reading しゃ , we use "shaman". There's a car . It's the nicest car you've ever seen. Exquisite, beautiful. Wouldn't you be surprised to learn it belongs to a sha man ( しゃ )? Well it does. This shaman charges a premium for his shaman services so he can afford fancy cars like this. Hints The more fantastic you make this car, the better. Also, feel the surprise of a shaman getting out of this car. What a cool dude that shaman is.

meaningMnemonic: The radical for center and the kanji for center are exactly the same. Hints That means if you know your radicals well, you know the meaning of this kanji as well! How swell.
readingMnemonic: Remember that guy from the 央 radical fastening his belt across the center of his body? This guy always secures his belt at the center — not slightly to the left, not slightly to the right, but dead center. His precision is so mind-blowing that everyone watching can't help but say, " Ohh !"( おう ). Hints Next time you put a belt on, make sure it's in the exact center of your body. Heck, try it now. And don't forget to say "Ohh!" as you do it. It'll keep the reading for this kanji front and center in your mind.

meaningMnemonic: The forehead of this beggar is on the ground . Except it's not exactly the ground, it's a giant copy machine, and he's making copies of his forehead! Hints Picture how ridiculous this beggar looks, making copies of his forehead with the ground copy machine.
readingMnemonic: This ground copy machine can only be the work of one person: a sha man ( しゃ )! Hints This particular shaman's specialty is being able to turn any surface into a copy machine with a twirl of his little shaman wand. Picture him running around in circles, doing a little dance and chant, and then the ground suddenly turning into one giant copy machine.

meaningMnemonic: The leader samurai didn't become leader by sitting around not taking action. He got to where he is by doing . Hints Imagine the leader samurai doing things. He's doing more than anyone else, no one can keep up with what he's doing.
readingMnemonic: He was doing things with shee p ( し ). He is the leader of the sheep clan, and he was able to do more with sheep than anyone else. That's why he's the leader. Hints Picture the leader samurai doing lots of sheep things. He's shearing sheep. He's feeding sheep. He's doing everything you could possibly do, because he's the sheep samurai.

meaningMnemonic: The ear radical and ear kanji are the same in looks as well as meaning. Hints Study those radicals hard to make sure you know your kanji as well!
readingMnemonic: Put your hand to your ear and sing... " Mimi mimimimiiiii!" ( みみ ) and listen to your tone with your ear. Hints This is sort of a stereotypical singer sort of image. Make sure you concentrate a lot when you're listening to your mimimimiiii tone. In fact, why don't you do it out loud right now - make a little fool of yourself. It's fun, and it'll help you to remember!

meaningMnemonic: When the sun is above the cross , it's time for some people to go church — which is always way too early on a Sunday, am I right? And if you want to get to church early, you need to be fast , otherwise you'll be too late. Hints Imagine the sun coming up slowly, over the horizon. It then lines up with the cross, and at that moment, your alarm goes off, waking you up. You check the alarm clock, and instead of displaying the time, it just says EARLY and FAST on it, flashing in big red letters and alternating.
readingMnemonic: To remember the そう reading we use the word "soul." When you're forced to get up fast and early you can feel it in your sou l ( そう ). You're so tired and it's so early, your soul cries out, "Please don't make me go this fast this early. I'm gonna leave your body if you keep this up!" Hints But you get your soul up early and head to the church fast anyway, because you're doing all of this for your soul in the first place!

meaningMnemonic: These days energy is the greatest treasure . Not gold, money, or anything like that. Imagine finding some in a literal treasure chest. As soon as you open it, out bursts the energy in a kind of spirit ball. Hints Touch the energy, catch the spirit ball. Is it solid or gaseous? Does it tingle or burn? Try to imagine it out. Then, yes, go ahead and sell that valuable energy treasure to a power company or something.
readingMnemonic: As you reach inside the energy spirit ball, you feel something hard inside. It's a large key ( き ) that gives you access to another treasure. Hints You take the key and open another treasure that's nearby. Open it up and see what's inside. Imagine something spectacular. Thanks, energy key.

meaningMnemonic: If you want to dry your horns you need to lay them flat . If they aren't flat they'll always be a little damp somewhere and you'll never have a moment's peace . Hints Imagine carefully taking off your horns and laying them flat on a paper towel. You have to smooth them out so they're as flat as possible.
readingMnemonic: Being flat isn't enough, so you cover the whole thing in hay ( へい ). Hay absorbs water, so you add a flat layer of it. Hints Imagine carefully laying a flat layer of hay on top of your flat horns. You feel really at peace and... you're tired now. You decided to lie on top of the hay and take a nap while you wait for your horns to dry.

meaningMnemonic: All these flowers were planted by your leader with nothing but a spoon . Now the whole place is absolutely full of beautiful flower s. Flowers everywhere. Hints Your leader is a nice guy who wants there to be flowers for future generations to enjoy. That's why he's painstakingly planting all these flowers with his spoon. Imagine watching him dig hole after hole with his little spoon just to plant some flowers for everyone.
readingMnemonic: Secretly, the leader is actually planting all these flower s for Hannah ( はな ), a girl he has a huge crush on. Everyone thinks the leader's a nice, selfless guy, but really he's just trying to impress Hannah. Hints You and everyone else are free to enjoy the flowers too, but… Just make sure to get out of the way when Hannah shows up. These flowers are really for her.

meaningMnemonic: The radical for foot and the kanji for foot are exactly the same. That said, there's another meaning you should keep in mind, which is sufficient . If you think about it, one foot should be sufficient enough to walk around with. You'd have to hop, but one foot is definitely still sufficient. Hints You know this kanji like the back of your foot by now, since it's the same as the radical. Still, try to remember the new "sufficient" meaning too.
readingMnemonic: What do you wear on your foot ? You wear a sock ( そく ). Hints Just think about your bare feet. Think about them too much. Feel how cold it is on your feet. Now, put on a sock to make it feel better. Ahhh, so nice!

meaningMnemonic: Take your fingers to the street to hit some people! Street fingers are for curling into a fist. And that street fist wants to do some hitting! Hints Imagine: it's just you, your fingers, and the wild street. It's hitting time!
readingMnemonic: As you hit one chump after another, suddenly your da d ( だ ) comes marching out of your house. Uh oh. Dad caught you hitting, which, honestly, isn't a very nice thing to do, so he has every right to stop you. Hints Now imagine your dad saying, "Don't do a hit!" over and over at you. "I'm sorry dad! But the streets were calling me!"

meaningMnemonic: The hole radical and the hole kanji are exactly the same! Spectacular!
readingMnemonic: Ana ( あな ) fell into a hole . Laugh at Ana and her unfortunate misfortune of having fallen into a hole like a ninny. Haha, Ana – you’re stupid and clumsy! Hints Imagine yourself laughing at Ana while you point at her, continuing to jeer as Ana struggles to escape the hole. You’d help Ana out of the hole, but you’re too busy laughing at her.

meaningMnemonic: There is a leaf growing out of the sun ! You fly out into space to check it out and when you get closer you see that it isn't just one leaf, it's a hundred ! That makes sense, you wouldn't be able to see just one leaf on the sun from where you were on earth. Hints Imagine flying toward the sun to see a hundred leaves growing together in the shape of one big leaf. You want to go closer!
readingMnemonic: You fly closer, counting all one hundred leaves when you hear a strange sound. You take off your space helmet and hear, "GUH HYUCK ( ひゃく )!" You know that laugh... it's Goofy! On top of the hundredth leaf is Goofy laughing and waving around. He must have built this leaf tower to get your attention. Hints Imagine hearing Goofy guh-hyuck over and over after you save him from being stranded on the sun. How would you feel being stuck in a cramped ship with laughing Goofy and his hundred leaves? Oh, you thought he would leave those behind? Nope, they saved him so you have to take them back too. Happy travels!

meaningMnemonic: Add a drop of something magical to water and suddenly it turns into big block of ice , just like that. Hints Imagine yourself adding that drop. What is it exactly? Something pretty potent, that's for sure. Now go ahead and touch the block of ice... wow, it's really cold — and only from one drop, too. Feel the burn on your finger from where you touched the ice .
readingMnemonic: When you think of ice , I want you to think of someone frozen with ice. Do you know anyone named Corey ( こおり )? Anyone famous named Corey, perhaps Corey Feldman? Imagine this Corey person frozen solid with ice. Hints How did this happen? Was it your fault? Imagine the situation that would get Corey frozen like this.

meaningMnemonic: The insect radical and insect are the same in looks as well as and meaning. Hints It's times like these when you gotta hope you're studying your radicals!
readingMnemonic: It's an insect ! Get it! You squish it with your foot - what sound does it make? A mush ( むし ) sound. Hints Imagine little words that say "mush" flying out from under your foot as you mush the poor thing. What does a "mush" sound sound like? You'll have to come up with something unique to yourself, and focus on it to remember this reading.

meaningMnemonic: The inside radical and the inside kanji are exactly the same, yay. But is the radical inside the kanji here, or is the kanji inside the radical? I don't know, it's inside-ception. Hints Hold that radical knowledge inside your head! It'll lure new kanji knowledge inside, like bait or something.
readingMnemonic: If you need to get inside something, the quickest way is to use a kni fe ( ない ). With a knife, you can cut something open and see what's inside it and within it. Hints Don't get any weird ideas — we're talking about using a knife to get inside bags and packages and stuff. If you imagined something else, that's on you. We can't take responsibility for whatever dark knife-related imagery you may have inside your head.

meaningMnemonic: The radical for man and the kanji for man are exactly the same. Hints That means if you know your radicals well, you know the meaning of this kanji too! Man, kanji are easy sometimes.
readingMnemonic: When you think of a man , think of dawn ( だん ), because that man has to get up at dawn to power his rice paddy every day. Hints Picture the man watching as the first light of dawn tints the sky pink and orange. Time to get to work, man!

meaningMnemonic: The radical master and the kanji master have the same meanings! This kanji also means main because the master is the main person of a dojo or household or business.
readingMnemonic: Do you remember back to the radical mnemonic, where the master is floating a water drop above his head? Imagine back to there. Once you do, the most amazing thing happens. The master sends the drop of water into a chu te ( しゅ ) and it goes careening through an intricate series of them. Hints Picture this master of water controlling the droplet as it flies around inside these chutes, like he's solving a difficult puzzle with it. Astounding!

meaningMnemonic: What is the evening mouth ? Imagine a mouth that's up in the night sky. It's just there, talking, and only comes out at night. It only appears in one area of the world. (What area would you choose? Imagine yourself going to that place to see the "evening mouth.") And it appears only one month out of the year (more on this in a second). The "evening mouth" is the most famous thing in the _____ area (this is the area you choose). He's so famous that everybody knows his name ("Evening Mouth"). Hints Imagine yourself going to the area you chose, and watching "Evening Mouth" speak. There are thousands of others there, wanting to see the giant floating mouth in the night sky. "Evening Mouth" then says "Everyone, what's my name ?!" and everyone shouts back "Evening Mouth!" in unison. "Evening Mouth" has certainly gotten really famous .
readingMnemonic: So, when does “Evening Mouth” appear? Turns out, “Evening Mouth” only comes out to talk in May ( めい ). You know this because it’s just starting to be spring, and when you look around (you’re watching “Evening Mouth” again) you see some spring flowers come up. Hints You know what they say. April showers bring May Flowers. What do May Flowers bring? They bring “Evening Mouth,” baby.

meaningMnemonic: The radical not and the kanji not are the same thing! That makes it easy... Not! Hints Actually, it does make it easy — the radicals make kanji wayyy easier, no?
readingMnemonic: To remember ふ we'll use the word "fool." Think of those jokes, where someone says something, then ends with a loud " NOTTTT !" Someone is doing that to you, over and over. What is that person? That person is a foo l ( ふ ). Hints Be sure to feel irritated at that person. Think in your head as they're telling these dumb "not" jokes how much of a fool they are... and how much of a fool you are for sitting here and listening to them.

meaningMnemonic: There's a mouth in the ground (in our case, it's a hatch), and inside is some kind of prison you can't quite get to. If you've ever seen Lost, this will sound familiar... on the hatch, there's actually a series of number s that you don't understand. Hints What are these numbers? What do they mean? Think over it for a while, get frustrated, and try to figure it out. You can't, though, so you probably won't ever get inside.
readingMnemonic: "You want to know the number to the hatch?" yells an old voice from inside. You say "yes," and the voice gives you the numbers and you're in! You go down into the prison, where there is one prisoner: Grandpa ごう いち . Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち . Hints Grandpa ごういち keeps saying numbers as you free him from the prison. Just one after another. Numbers numbers numbers. Hopefully old man ごういち isn't crazy.

meaningMnemonic: The origin radical and the origin kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals!
readingMnemonic: The origin of everything can be found in Gen ji ( げん ). Genji is the name of the main character in the world's first ever novel, "The Tale of Genji." Picture him as a rich, pretty boy who cares a ton about his looks and gets along really well with all the ladies. He's also really great at poetry, which helps the lady situation. Hints Genji's origin story is pretty important when it comes to mnemonics and Japanese literature. He's going to keep popping up on your kanji journey, so make sure you remember him!

meaningMnemonic: The leader of alligators ... she's no ordinary leader, that's for sure. She's not a politician, she's not a queen... She's one of the Other Ones, a group of strange, eccentric people who become leaders of animals. Hints Imagine different groups of leaders — they're all dressed nice and normal. Then, off to the side are the leaders of bears, cats, alligators, and narwhals... They're the other ones, no matter how you look at it. They are in their own group, and they are considered "others" because society won't accept them :(
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading た , we use the word "taco": Then there's the other s of the others. These are the ta co ( た ) worshipers. They're really strange. Hints Just imagine the "others" shaking their heads at these taco worshipers. Seriously, what the heck?

meaningMnemonic: If someone tries to dig up dirt on your private life, tell them no thanks, that stuff is in the past . Some things should stay in the past. Not everyone needs to know everything about your life and your past. Hints Keep your private dirt in the past. It's better for everyone.
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading きょ , we'll use "Little Kyoto." This will differentiate きょ from きょう , which is regular-sized Kyoto. Get it? You decide to bury all this private dirt from your past in Little Kyo to ( きょ ). That stuff is from when you were just a little 子 ( こ ) and you don't like to think about it. Hints Imagine physically, literally burying your past 子 self. If you hide it in Little Kyoto, no one will ever be able to dig it up.

meaningMnemonic: The plate kanji and the plate radical are exactly the same, like two matching pieces of china. Hints If you know your radicals, you know your kanji too.
readingMnemonic: The person washing all the dish es was named Sarah ( さら ). She was named that because of her large head, which was shaped like Sarah Jessica Parker’s head (very big). Hints Imagine someone with a huge head, washing dishes. When I say huge, I mean huge. She turns towards you with her big head and says “Hi, I’m Sarah” and you see her name tag, which also says Sarah. She is Sarah, the dish washer. The plates she holds up next to her head pale in comparison, even though they're the biggest pieces.

meaningMnemonic: If you go down a slide and get dirt on your legs , it must have been the fault of the previous person, aka the person who went down the slide ahead of you. They should've cleaned off their dirty legs before they went down the slide, but they didn't, and now you've got dirt all over your legs too. Hints Try to imagine the previous person — they must have been absolutely filthy to leave all this dirt behind. Why'd they have to go down the slide ahead of you?! If only you could've gotten here before them…
readingMnemonic: Then you realize: the previous person on the slide must've been a cen taur ( せん ). Centaurs track dirt everywhere 'cause they're always galloping around in the wilderness. Hints If you look really far off into the distance ahead of you, you might still be able to spot this dirty, slide-ruining centaur. Hurry up and go after him before he gets on another slide!

meaningMnemonic: The radical for red and the kanji for red are the same thing! Hints What a lucky ducky — as long as you know your radicals, you'll know this kanji's meaning as well!
readingMnemonic: This kanji means red , AKA , also known as, あか . Hints Think of あか as being some sort of alias for "red." That's why it's pronounced あか in Japanese, AKA "red."

meaningMnemonic: The leader is next to the tree . What is he doing? He's leaning against it, rest ing. Hints The best thing to do with a tree is rest under it. Picture the leader resting under the tree with his eyes half closed.
readingMnemonic: As he rest s, he suddenly gets hungry and pulls a cu cumber ( きゅう ) off the tree and bites into it. A good rest isn't complete without some crunchy tree cucumbers. Hints Don't email me saying cucumbers don't grow on trees. Cucumber trees exist. Look them up and then rest easy knowing I'd never lie to you.

meaningMnemonic: There's a cross inside your mouth , so the things you say are very pious. Everything you say, you say humbly . Hints Imagine yourself with a cross inside your mouth, saying all kinds of humble things. "Oh no, I'm not that good." "Oh no, my mustache doesn't look that great."
readingMnemonic: As you're saying all these humble things, you're also mow ing ( もう ) your neighbor's lawn. Your neighbors love you so much, because you're so humble, and you mow their lawn for them. Hints Imagine mowing your neighbor's lawn while you say humbly how bad you are at mowing lawns. What a good neighbor you are.

meaningMnemonic: The radical see and the kanji see are exactly the same! Hints Make sure you study your radicals. If you do, you'll know a lot of kanji as well, almost magically.
readingMnemonic: You see something. It's walking towards you, but you need to see better. When the person comes close, you realize, "That person is me ( み )!" Hints The struggling-to-see bit is pretty important — make sure that you slowly see a little better as the person comes closer, but it's difficult the whole time (struggles are good for memory). Then, it starts to become more and more clear, and you start saying, "That can't be me . No way it's me..." When the person comes up to you (the person also being you) you learn about parallel universes and other fabulous things. Still, the whole time you can't stop thinking, "This person looks just like me... No, this person is me!"

meaningMnemonic: The shellfish radical and the shellfish kanji are the same! It can be just the shell part too. Hints Shellfish are shellfish, you know?
readingMnemonic: To get some shellfish , all you have to do is hop in your kay ak ( かい ) and get some. Shellfish live in the water. Hints Imagine rowing your kayak out into the ocean to collect shellfish. Imagine the color and shape of the kayak. Feel the spray of the salt water and the taste of some fresh shellfish, right out of the ocean.

meaningMnemonic: The stone radical and stone kanji are the same thing! Hints Know your radicals and therefore know your kanji. It's just that simple.
readingMnemonic: You throw a stone through a window... and now, you can see something very sexy ( せき ). Hints Whoops, maybe you shouldn't throw stones through windows, or you'll see people's sexy times.

meaningMnemonic: What do you get if you lend a spirit your umbrella ? Thanks , of course! Especially if that spirit is Totoro, the spirit of the forest. Hints It's raining, so you lend Totoro your umbrella. As thanks, he gives you a present wrapped in bamboo leaves.

readingMnemonic: All of this treasure is kept in the king's ho me ( ほう ). He can't let other people see how much treasure he has, or they'll get mad. Or worse, ask him to share some with his people. meaningMnemonic: Someone's taking tree measurements … Why are they taking measurements of trees? Because they're planning to cut them down to make their village . The mural is of the forest where they got the trees from, to honor the village's origins. Hints Look at the mural on the side of this newly constructed village center. So many trees! Visualize the whole process of the tree becoming a building, as you reflect on the message of the mural.

meaningMnemonic: Fourth day or day four . No matter how you look at this combination of kanji, the meaning of the word makes a lot of sense!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Counting days, however, is an exception (at least up to ten). You need to use the kun'yomi readings to read this word. You already know the kun'yomi reading for 四 , so that's fine (the ん gets turned into a small っ , though). Think of it this way: On the fourth day of being lost in the wilderness, you start yelling " Yo , ca r ( よっか )!" out of desperation, never getting an answer. meaningMnemonic: The master person isn't just a master. You have to think back to when they were making these kanji. Who was the master? It was the head of household . Because, I guess the head of household back in the day was the husband. Those sexist ancient people!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: In Japan, tradition says the head of a household must slide down a chu te in only jean s ( しゅじん ). Whenever you need to speak to the head of the household, they'll come sliding down a chute wearing nothing but jeans. What a sight!

The image is momentum: doing something in a single burst, rather than something happening instantaneously.

The first key lets you out onto the veranda, where you do the actual moon viewing, and the second key unlocks your pantry full of moon-viewing snacks. meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This word is generally added to the end of a number, as in 三号 ("number 3"). readingMnemonic: This word is made up of a single kanji all alone, but it uses the on'yomi reading. This is probably because you'll usually see this word attached to other things, like numbers. meaningMnemonic: A stop that's just a rest (aka not permanent) isn't a straight up stop. You're planning on continuing again. That's why this is a pause , suspension , or hiatus . This is a fairly formal word, and it's often used when an activity or a service is temporarily suspended. For example, you could use it to talk about a class being suspended, a machine suspending its operation, or a pop band going on a hiatus. Check out the context section for more example usages.

meaningMnemonic: This is a pretty old word, and in the olden days, everything was cut by hand , including postage stamp s. Having to cut thousands of stamp s each day by hand sounds incredibly laborious, so maybe that's why this word came to be associated specifically with stamps.

Naturally, kids use small plates when they have their meals, because they themselves are small, and the food they eat is small, and it fits on small plates. meaningMnemonic: You learned 文字 means "letter (of the alphabet)" or "character." And what does the kanji character for one look like in Japanese? A straight line ! Think of this word as meaning "the 一 character." In Japanese, it's most often used to describe the straight line a person's lips make when they're pressed together in concentration, frustration, or silence.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 文 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Anyone who goes around with his mouth in a straight line is probably a mon ster ( もん ). How could anyone walk around with such an uninviting expression on their face? Basically, anyone who isn't smiling constantly is a monster, as far you're concerned. And that includes those monsters with 一文字 -shaped mouths.

meaningMnemonic: Everything that happened to you previous ly is just the tip of the iceberg, and the important stuff is ahead of you, in your future . So make sure you put that stuff first ! The original meaning of this word is the tip of something, like a pen or a finger. From that meaning, it's expanded into all sorts of meanings, like "ahead," "first," and "future," depending on the context and where it is in the sentence. It can also mean "previous" in formal contexts (and we'll accept that meaning too, but we're not teaching it here because it's more advanced).
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it uses the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with the kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Just ahead of you are the tip s of a saw and a key ( さき ). You have no idea what they're doing there, but both saws and keys have very sharp tips, so watch out you don't hurt yourself. Imagine yourself edging carefully past those saw and key tips. P.S. You can differentiate this from 先ず ( まず ) because it doesn't have any hiragana on the end.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means leg or sufficient , and we're going with the "sufficient" meaning for this word! This word means to be enough .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading.
